entries.title: Who is responsible for the Ceuta border surge?
entries.summary: Tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta several days ago. DW interviewed two experts to understand what may have caused the incident.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

Tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta several days ago. DW interviewed two experts to understand what may have caused the incident.

For a long time, the Moroccan government chose not to comment on the Ceuta border crisisthat saw tens of thousands of migrants surging into the Spanish exclave on the African continent. It was not until Sunday that Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi said "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling were to blame for the incident. Morocco has since said it never intended for the border surge to happen and has promised full cooperation with Spain.

Spain, however, was quick to suspect Moroccan involvement, with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calling the border breach an "attack on our territorial sovereignty." Videos have, after all, surfaced showing Moroccan security forces doing nothing to stop the crowd surging forward.

Efforts have been made to try and explain what caused the migrant crisis. Some have said Spain's recent rapprochement with Algeria may have angered Marocco, while others have speculated US influence may have played a role, although there is no reliable evidence to support the latter theory.

A complex situation

DW spoke with two analysts who caution against simplistic explanations. They do, however, ascribe different degrees of responsibility to Marocco for causing the crisis.

"I think the situation today is significantly different from what it was in 2021," says Isabelle Werenfels, a Maghreb regional expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). Back then, Morocco was interested in exerting foreign policy pressure on Spain over the Western Sahara dispute, she says. Today, Moroccowould have "a great deal to lose, above all, international credibility and investment" if found to have deliberately orchestrated the Ceuta migrant surge.

Jochen Oltmer, a migration researcher at the University of Osnabrück in Germany, also warns against jumping to conclusions, telling DW "you have to keep in mind the many different interests at play." He points to Ceuta's unique status as a European exclave on the African continent, decades of migration flows, the impact of social networks, and the hopes of many migrants to build better lives abroad.

Oltmer says Moroccan authorities carry considerable responsibility for the Ceuta crisis, as "such a border crossing could never have taken place if the Moroccan side hadn't looked the other way." It was this inaction that made possible a border breach of this magnitude in the first place, he told DW.

Werenfels does not dispute this assessment. Yet she also believes Morocco may have wanted to send a political signal to Spain, perhaps over its recent rapprochement with Algeria and its decision to grant Spanish citizenship to individuals born in Western Sahara before September 1977.

"But there is a significant difference between making a political statement and orchestrating a migration surge on this scale," Werenfels says. The expert thinks it is "unlikely" that Morocco had planned the latter, even though it cannot be ruled out, while stressing a lot of information remains extremely unclear-

Who bears responsibility?

There is some evidence to suggest that Morocco played a part in the border surge to push its own political agenda, says Oltmer. For years, the country has viewed itself as an indispensable partner to the European Union in the context of migration policy, he says, adding that Morocco has repeatedly emphasized how much the bloc depends on its cooperation. Yet the conflict over Western Sahara, and Morocco's rivalry with Algeria, also plays an important role, Oltmer explains. That is why he "ultimately cannot imagine that the recent events would have been possible without Morocco."

Werenfels advocates for a more nuanced analysis. She suspects it's possible that Morocco wanted to send a message but that matters got out of control. Werenfels says it is hard to imagine that Morocco would want to risk a lasting rift with Spain and the European Union. This is all the more true given that Morocco will be hosting the next football World Cup together with Spain and Portugal, and also depends on Spanish gas supplies. In 2025, one-quarter of Spain's total natural gas exports went to Morocco.

Even if Morocco had wanted to send a political message, that does not automatically mean that it deliberately orchestrated a migration surge of this magnitude, Werenfels says. Doing so would carry enormous political and economic risk.

No evidence of third-party involvement

Neither of the experts believe a third country played a part in the Ceuta migration crisis. That said, Werenfels does entertain the possibility that other governments or political actors may have attempted to exploit the situation propagandistically for their own political interests and thereby may have amplified the crisis.

Werenfels also says it remains unclear how the situation escalated so quickly. There is much to suggest that news of an alleged border opening spread very quickly, prompting numerous young Moroccans to spontaneously set off for Ceuta. It is also possible that, given these circumstances, some Moroccan security personnel did not intervene.

Both scholars agree on the root causes of migration. "It's about hope and expectations for the future," says Oltmer. Moroccans have been emigrating for many decades, with family and friendship networks in Europe making it easier for people to risk moving abroad, he says.

Werenfels also points out social and economic factors driving emigration. She says that while Morocco had made progress in recent years, many young people are hardly seeing improvements in their everyday lives. The scholar says Marocco's education and health care sectors show particularly significant shortcomings. This lack of prospects compels many to risk migrating abroad, Werenfels says.

Overall, both experts agree that the Ceuta migrant crisis was not brought about by a single political decision, or conspiracy theory, for that matter. The incident instead resulted from the interplay of geopolitical tensions, migration policy agendas, and the often precarious circumstances of many young Moroccans.

This article was translated from German

entries.title: Middle East: India says commercial ship sunk off Yemen
entries.summary: India reported an attack on a "defenseless" commercial ship which caused it to capsize and sink, but noted the crew were safe. Meanwhile, Lebanon and Israel met for talks despite Hezbollah's objections. DW has more.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Middle East: India says commercial ship sunk off Yemen

Published August 4, 2026last updated August 4, 2026

India reported an attack on a "defenseless" commercial ship which caused it to capsize and sink, but noted the crew were safe. Meanwhile, Lebanon and Israel met for talks despite Hezbollah's objections. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India reports commercial ship struck and sunk off Yemeni coast, says crew all rescued
  • Hezbollah and Lebanon's government clash over latest talks with Israel
  • Representatives of the two governments are meeting at the US Embassy in Rome
  • The Trump administration claims, once again, it is close to a breakthrough in talks with Iran
  • Follow DW for updates on the US-Iran war and the wider conflicts in the Middle East on Tuesday, August 4. 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section India: Continuing attacks on shipping 'deeply worrisome'

India: Continuing attacks on shipping 'deeply worrisome'

India's Foreign Ministry called for restoring free and safe navigation.

"The continuing incidents of attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply worrisome," the ministry said.

"The targeting of commercial shipping in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways in the region, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," it said.

India is a major importer of oil, petroleum, natural gas and other goods from the Gulf region, and is directly connected to the region via the Arabian Sea. It is therefore one of the countries hardest hit by the economic disruption from the US-Iran war.

India currently contributes more than 300,000 seafarers to the global shipping industry, which is more than 10% of the global total, second only to the Philippines.

Skip next section India reports 'defenseless' ship struck and sunk off Yemen

India reports 'defenseless' ship struck and sunk off Yemen

An Indian vessel has been struck near Yemeni waters, India Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on Tuesday.

"Indian MSV Faize Noore Oliya has been hit by a projectile near Yemeni waters, causing the vessel to capsize and sink," Sonowal said, without attributing responsibility.

"India strongly condemns this unprovoked attack on the defenseless mechanized sailing vessel. The safety of our people is our supreme priority and I am relieved to inform that ALL 14 seafarers (including 13 Indians) have been safely rescued by the Yemeni Coast Guard and brought to the Port of Mokha," he wrote.

Sonowal said he had instructed the country's Director General Maritime Admnistration to take "immediate steps" and "ensure the absolute security of Indian seafarers in the region."

India's Foreign Ministry also condemned the incident in a statement, and said its Embassy in Riyadh was "closely monitoring the situation and proactively coordinating with Yemeni authorities." 

Concerns over shipping off Yemen's coast — approaching the western coast of Saudi Arabia and the Red Sea, rather than the Persian Gulf — has come into increased focus in recent weeks since the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen declared a "blockade" of Saudi Arabia and told commercial ships to avoid the area.

Skip next section Rubio: US 'involved' in Iran-Oman Hormuz talks

Rubio: US 'involved' in Iran-Oman Hormuz talks

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared to shed some light on alleged talks with Iran following conflicting messages from Washington and Tehran.

After Trump had suggested talks with Iran were progressing, Iran had instead said it was talking with Oman about trying to allow shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, in turn, dubbed this "unbelievably duplicitous!" online.

A day later, Rubio said that talks were indeed taking place between Iran and Oman, but also said that the US was "involved" in the process.

"There's been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet. We're hoping that will happen very shortly," Rubio told reporters at the State Department.

Skip next section Cargo vessel catches fire after projectile strike off Oman

Cargo vessel catches fire after projectile strike off Oman

A commercial vessel was struck "by an unknown projectile" overnight off the coast of Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Tuesday.

It listed the location as a site either in or near the Strait of Hormuz, some 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) northeast of Al Khasab in Oman. 

The UKMTO did not identify the vessel or provide information about possible damage, but a maritime security company provided more information later.

Vanguard Tech identified the ship as a Liberia-flagged bulk carrier, called the "Minoan Pioneer," and said it was transiting northbound through the strait at the time of the attack.

"The projectile reportedly struck the engine room, while a fire broke out in the accommodation area. The crew are fighting the fire and require assistance, while the third engineer is reported missing," Vanguard said.

It said another ship filed the initial distress call, reporting that the affected vessel had suffered a "complete blackout and required assistance."

Skip next section US Treasury Secretary Bessent touts 'chance' of deal 'today or tomorrow'

US Treasury Secretary Bessent touts 'chance' of deal 'today or tomorrow'

Members of Donald Trump's administration are backing up the US president's claims of progress with Iran.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a media interview on Tuesday that a deal securing Strait of Hormuz shipping could be struck as early as this week. 

"We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalized position in this conflict," Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC.

When asked if the deal would include Strait of Hormuz transit fees demanded by Tehran, Bessent also said he expected ships would be able to pass freely.

Iran had disputed Donald Trump's claims of talks with the US altogether on Monday, instead saying it was negotiating with Oman and hoping for a deal on commercial shipping.

Skip next section Hezbollah and Lebanon's government clash over Israel talks

Hezbollah and Lebanon's government clash over Israel talks

Israeli and Lebanese negotiators met in Rome on Tuesday for a seventh round of US-sponsored direct talks, seeking to implement plans to remove Israel's military from its unilaterally imposed "buffer zone" near the de facto border. 

Even as the talks took place, however, the powerful Iran-backed militia Hezbollah expressed their opposition to the process, casting doubt on the government in Beirut's ability to implement any agreements reached. 

"All the direct negotiations will bring Lebanon nothing but shame, humiliation, disappointment and successive concessions," Hezbollah's chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address.

He alleged that President Joseph Aoun "has not acted as an arbiter, nor as a unifying figure, but has become biased and divisive, which is incompatible with his role and with Lebanon's strength."

Lebanon's Prime Minister Naim Sawaf fired back in a post online, saying that "the greatest help to Israel was provided by those who uniltareally drew Lebanon into the adventures of futile wars ... and granted pretexts to attack our country."

Lebanon's government attempted to ordered Hezbollah not to attack Israel in response to the US-Israeli strikes on Iran but the attempt failed.

The talks in Rome are seeking to replace the Israeli military in southern Lebanese towns and villages with Lebanese troops, who should in turn pledge to disarm Hezbollah fighters and prevent them from attacking sites in northern Israel. The places where it takes effect are being called "pilot zones."

It was not clear how the Lebanese government plans to secure or enforce Hezbollah's cooperation. Germany, the US, Israel and others regard the Shiite militia as a terror group.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to our updates on the conflicts in the Middle East on Tuesday, August 4, 2026.

The latest round of US-brokered talks between Israel and Lebanon are taking place in Rome, albeit to the apparent displeasure of the Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. 

Meanwhile, the news on the talks between the US and Iran is less clear. The Trump administration is reporting a resumption of negotiations and indeed progress as it attempts to secure guarantees on the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has been much more reticent, speaking only of bilateral discussions with Oman.

Amid the back and forth, another commercial vessel came under fire near the Strait of Hormuz overnight, with a fire breaking out on board.

We will be bringing you more on these and other stories from the Middle East in this live blog.

entries.title: South Sudan: How climate change can result in toxic water
entries.summary: Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the crisis is yet to emerge.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the crisis is yet to emerge.

The village of Bentiu has seen it all: Located in the north of South Sudan near the border with Sudan, the capital of Unity State used to have a population of merely several thousand people.

But war, violence and other crisis have resulted in an additional 140,000 displaced persons seeking shelter there since 2013, resulting in the establishment of a massive camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs).

Several UN bodies including the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) are active on the ground, running what is known as the Protection of Civilians (POC) camp, which by now feels more like a permanent structure.

At a makeshift pier, children are seen playing, countless canoes bring in fish to feed scores of people at the camp, where food insecurity remains a chief concern.

Immediately, each day's yield is separated into two categories: One stock with fresh, healthy fish, and another for those believed to be contaminated.

Simon Gatkuoth, a camp resident in his early forties, lifts a fish from a wheelbarrow, explaining that fish that are caught near the oil fields are contaminated: "When we cook them, the soup sometimes smells like penicillin," he says.

"But there is no option. We have to eat. We cannot stop eating because there is no alternative."

Flood waters that just won't recede

Viewed from the sky, the POC Camp resembles an artificial island in the midst of a region that has been transformed into what appears to be a gigantic lake.

Here, the largely nomadic communities of South Sudan's Unity State have long adapted their lives to the seasonal floods that shape life in what is one of the world's largest wetlands known as the Sudd.

But in 2021, and unprecedented deluge of floods linked to climate change submerged farmland across the region, destroying livelihoods and killing thousands of cattle.

Just one year earlier, authorities in neighboring Uganda had issued a warning that rising levels in Lake Victoria, situated roughly 1,000 kilometers (650 miles) to the south, would require the release of large volumes of water into the White Nile river, which flows past Bentiu.

But South Sudan, one of the poorest countries, lacked the dams, flood-control systems and water-management infrastructure needed to cope with the flooding, leaving many communities highly vulnerable to flooding.

To this day, the waters from that flood are yet to recede.

Oil and water do not mix

Maintained by the IOM, a simple levee is all that separates the POC Camp from the flooded plain; without constant maintenance, it would give way to the water.

The people here appear weary: First displaced by war and later hit by floods, most now depend on humanitarian aid, trapped somewhere between continuously rising water levels and unresolved conflict.

Yet in recent years, another disaster has slowly emerged, linking the devastating 2021 flooding to a major environmental hazard: Unity State, where the Bentiu POC Camp is located, is the South Sudan's biggest oil producing region.

Oil makes up more than 90% of state revenue, and accounts for nearly all of the country's exports. It is a vital sector for the country's battling economy, which has been severely limited in recent years by the war in Sudan to its north, with pipelines limited to a trickle, and many reserves sitting untapped or unused.

A geospatial analysis found that during the devastating 2021 floods, 159 out of over 400 oil wells in the region were submerged under water, amounting to around 41% of oil extraction infrastructure in the area.

In a joint effort with PlaceMarks Africa — an organization which makes of satellite imagery to help "design solutions for contemporary challenges" on the continent, DW has found that more than 50 of these wells continue to be submerged to this day — a growing cause for concern.

The rivers and lakes that hundreds of thousands depend on for drinking water, cooking and fishing appear to have been contaminated by the oil fields, with could carry potentially long-term consequences for both local ecosystems and human health.

"Many animals are dying because of this pollution, and people are also suffering from symptoms they attribute to it. All of this is visible, but we do not yet have sufficient evidence or epidemiological studies to state it with certainty," explains researcher Marko Gatkuoth, who is attached to the Rift Valley Institute — an independent research organization operating primarily in Central and Eastern Africa.

"The flood that began more than four years ago has become a vector of pollution. It has made the contaminants mobile."

'Deliberate negligence'

Bul Duot Kuer, a South Sudanese researcher at Kenyatta University in Kenya, has conducted extensive research on the environmental impact of oil production in Unity State.

In a recent study, he identified lead concentrations of up to 18 micrograms per liter in the rivers around Bentiu and nearby Rotriak — nearly double the guideline value set by the World Health Organization (WHO). He also found hydrocarbon concentrations in the water at more than five times above the recommended limits.

"Water is the most polluted element," says Kuer. "There is no control. The environmental laws are there on paper, but they are simply not being enforced. This is negligence. The government and the oil companies do not care about people's health."

Waters around the settlement of Rotriak are particularly affect by this oil contamination: Satellite imagery analysed by PlaceMarks exposed pipelines, wells and abandoned facilities scattered across the settlement.

This is an area were children play among rusty pipes and women wash laundry at a former retention pond for oil production wastewater — albeit typically not by choice: Local resident Anna Nyashing Bul told DW that she and her family had to evacuate to Rotriak "because it was the only place that remained dry" after the 2021 flooding.

The untreated water they rely on often has "black film on the surface," she explains, which has repeatedly made her family fall sick.



"But we had nothing else to drink."

Birth defects and miscarriages

Meanwhile at Bentiu State Hospital, staff have noticed an increase of children born with deformities and other birth defects.

Midwives interviewed by DW also describe an apparent increase in miscarriages, complicated deliveries and congenital anomalies in recent years — especially with mothers who come from areas located in and around the oil fields.

19-year-old Nyapuka Nios from Rotriak just gave birth days ago; her newborn presents visible malformations to the hands and upper lip.

"I don't know what will happen to him," she whispers. "It is God's will. God gave him to me this way."

In another room, Nyekal Nuok watches over her baby girl, who was born with spina bifida five days earlier. She also lived in Rotriak during most of her pregnancy.

Research has shown that women living near oil wells are more likely to give birth to children with congenital anomalies. 

Dorgan Patai, Director of Health Services in Rubkona County agrees that "since the floods, we are seeing more miscarriages and more children born with malformations," adding that "in the long term, this could even lead to infertility."

However, there has been no comprehensive investigation to establish whether these cases are indeed linked to environmental contamination.

The WHO says that a review of routine health surveillance data failed to present any statistically relevant increase in miscarriages, complications or other anomalies in Unity State, stressing that anecdotal reports should be interpreted cautiously.

Dead in the water

There are few people who have done more to hold South Sudanese authorities accountable for the environmental consequences of oil production than Ayen Mijok Kiir, First Deputy Speaker of the Council of States, which is South Sudan's upper house of parliament.

She believes that years of conflict and insecurity have pushed issues like environmental protection and public health down the list of national priorities.

"We are not a stable country," Kiir highlights. "There are challenges in allocating resources to different sectors. We are under pressure to prioritise security. But yes, even with these challenges, we should have done more."

With her tireless campaigning, she succeeded in encouraging President Salva Kiir to further investigate the potential link between deformities at birth and oil-related pollution in 2024 despite many other ongoing crises in the region.

But despite numerous ministerial meetings being held, nothing seems to change.

"What difference will it make if I talk about this yet again?" she s ays quietly. "I have spoken about it so much, given so many interviews, and nothing has happened."

Ultimately, South Sudan still lacks effective environmental monitoring and public health standard in its oil producing areas — 15 years after gaining independence.

With conflict and suffering remaining rife throughout the region, addressing the affects of global warming might remain an elusive goal, as South Sudan struggles on many fronts to keep its head above water.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

This project was supported by the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting

entries.title: What does Zambia's opposition stand without Edgar Lungu?
entries.summary: The death of former President Edgar Lungu reshaped opposition politics in Zambia ahead of the August 13 general election. Analysts say the vote will test whether his legacy can keep opposition supporters united.
entries.content:
Zambia

Where does Zambia's opposition stand without Edgar Lungu?

August 4, 2026

The death of former President Edgar Lungu reshaped opposition politics in Zambia ahead of the August 13 general election. Analysts say the vote will test whether his legacy can keep opposition supporters united.

Zambia's opposition is entering the 2026 general election without Edgar Lungu, the politician who for years united its biggest parties and inspired much of its support. Lungu, the country's former president, died in South Africa on June 5, 2025.

Opposition parties have since been competing to inherit his political legacy while trying to convince voters they remain a credible alternative to incumbent Hakainde Hichilema's ruling United Party for National Development (UPND).

Lungu had led the now dismantled Patriotic Front (PF) party, a faction of which became part of Zambia's overall opposition Tonse Alliance in 2024. The former president had also intitially been fronted as the coalition's 2026 presidential candidate.

'The Edgar Lungu factor is still at play'

Political analyst Neo Simutanyi says Lungu's absence exposes an unresolved leadership question within the opposition coalition.

"He had a Plan B. He intended to back someone who would carry forward his political project, but he never had the opportunity to announce that person before he died," Simutanyi told DW.

Competing claims emerged over who should lead the Tonse Alliance emerged after Lungu's death. The coalition, now rebranded as the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, has endorsed Brian Mundubile as its 2026 presidential candidate. He and Lungu were PF allies, while his running mate, Makebi Zulu, was Lungu's lawyer. Mundubile is widely seen as Hichilema's top challenger.

Simutanyi believes Lungu's influence nevertheless remains significant. "It is effectively a PF campaign without the PF label," he said, adding that several candidates are appealing to the same support base by presenting themselves as heirs to Lungu's legacy.

"The Edgar Lungu factor is still at play because candidates are campaigning on his legacy and many of the areas where he enjoyed strong support remain politically competitive."

A battle for voters

Lungu's influence remains particularly visible on the Copperbelt, Zambia's mining heartland and one of the country's most competitive electoral battlegrounds.

"Edgar Lungu's absence has left a big vacuum in the opposition, especially in the Patriotic Front. He was the one holding the party together," said Agness Tembo, a young leader from the Copperbelt.

She warned that a fragmented opposition could weaken Zambia's competitive multiparty democracy. But not all voters believe personalities will decide the election.

Richard Mwamba, another Copperbelt resident, said many people are more concerned about their daily lives than political succession. "This election will be less about personalities and more about delivery — jobs, the cost of living, mining, electricity, roads and the prices of goods and services," he said.

For many PF supporters, however, Lungu's absence remains deeply felt. "Lungu united people from different political backgrounds. It will be difficult to find someone with the same influence," said supporter Mabvuto Phiri.

Tonse Pamodzi Alliance Secretary-General Celestine Mukandila rejects suggestions that the coalition has lost momentum. "President Lungu had once indicated that he had a Plan B. Today I can confirm that the Plan B is in place," Mukandila told DW. The alliance remains united behind Mundubile, he added.

"We are responding to president Lungu's call for unity of purpose and now have an opportunity to elect Brian Mundubile as president."

A regional test

Analysts say Zambia's opposition now faces a challenge seen elsewhere in Southern Africa, where parties have struggled after losing dominant leaders.

In Zimbabwe, opposition politics became increasingly fragmented following the death of Morgan Tsvangirai in 2018, while leadership transitions in other countries have also tested the ability of parties to remain united and electorally competitive.

Zambia has held regular multiparty elections since 1991 and is widely regarded as one of the region's more stable democracies. The election this year, analysts say, will show whether opposition parties can broaden their appeal beyond one influential political figure.

Lungu came to power in a special presidential election upon the death of then President Michael Sata in 2015. The following year, he was reelected to a five-year term. After losing power to Hichilema in a 2021 vote, Lungu returned to frontline politics and became the opposition's most influential leader.

Simutanyi says Lungu's political influence did not end with his death. His name may no longer appear on the ballot, but the contest over his legacy could still shape how many Zambians vote on August 13.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

entries.title: EU agrees to send border aid to Spain after Ceuta talks
entries.summary: The Schengen Area was "in no way" compromised during the Ceuta incursion, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said after a video conference with his EU colleagues.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

The Schengen Area was "in no way" compromised during the Ceuta incursion, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said after a video conference with his EU colleagues.

European Union interior ministers emerged from a video conference on Tuesday with an agreement to beef up external security, the group said in a statement.

"There was a common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight," they wrote in a press release.

Ministers also "pointed out that communication during moments of crisis could further be reinforced through timely coordination and should be more coherent, especially to counter malicious external actors engaged in foreign information manipulation and interference."

The group agreed to provide emergency aid to Spain to help boost border security.

What happened in Ceuta?

The meeting had been called to address concerns about security inside the Schengen free movement area after some 60,000 people rushed the border gates in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.

Hundreds among the group were minors, European NGOs have said.

The incident prompted a series of blistering critiques from center-right and right-wing leaders of EU member states against left-leaning Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. Countries such as Italy and Finland called for an immediate suspension of Spain's membership in the Schengen agreement.

However, officials and law enforcement from across the EU have said that the breakdown of border controls was due to misinformation given to asylum seekers waiting on the border. Authorities also expressed suspicions that human trafficking gangs purposely misled the would-be migrants.

Spain's Ceuta exclave is located on the African continent, bordered by Morocco on one side and the sea on the other. It is subject to stricter-than-usual Schengen entry and exit procedures, as well as identity checks for passengers crossing over to the Spanish mainland.

Spain confirmed on Tuesday that some 60,000 people have returned to Morocco since the weekend, leaving 2,500 still in Ceuta.

What did EU interior ministers say?

"It is clear that in no way was the Schengen area compromised in this crisis," Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said after the talks with his counterparts in other EU nations.

His sentiment was echoed by French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez: "We all agreed the Schengen area was not really the problem."

European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said that there was "full solidarity with Spain around the table" at the meeting. He added that increased border security provided by the EU's Frontex agency was already active in Ceuta and "ready to do more."

He called the meeting a "useful opportunity" to confirm that no one had moved from Ceuta to the mainland.

"These past few days were a test of our European resilience, a test of the security of our external borders," Brunner told. "Europe, I think, has definitely passed this test."

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Is Bangladesh backtracking on post-Hasina reforms?
entries.summary: Two years after a student-led uprising toppled PM Sheikh Hasina, critics say Bangladesh's reform momentum is fading as political divisions deepen and key changes stall.
entries.content:
Bangladesh

Is Bangladesh backtracking on post-Hasina reforms?

August 4, 2026

Two years after a student-led uprising toppled PM Sheikh Hasina, critics say Bangladesh's reform momentum is fading as political divisions deepen and key changes stall.

Just two years after a student-led uprising ended the nearly 16-year rule of Sheikh Hasina, many fear Bangladesh is slipping backward.

With Hasina, now in exile in India, planning a return in December and critics accusing the current government of failing to deliver on its promises, the country's political future is once again in doubt.

"At the end of the day, we did not see the elimination of discrimination, the creation of an inclusive society, or the new political order that was promised," Mohammad Tanzimuddin Khan, a professor of international relations at Dhaka University, told DW.

"It seems we are forgetting the very reasons behind the uprising of last July, especially those who came to power."

The protest movement began in 2018 over a controversial quota system for government jobs. In 2024, a court-backed move to reinstate parts of the system sparked fresh demonstrations that grew into a wider anti-government uprising.

In August 2024, after more than 1,000 people were killed in the unrest, then Prime Minister Hasina fled to India.

Rebuilding Bangladesh's institutions

Bangladesh's interim government, which was led by Nobel Peace Prize winner Muhammad Yunus and backed by the military and key figures from the uprising, facilitated the signing of a reform roadmap. It was named the "July Charter" after the month when the uprising that toppled Hasina began. 

In a February 2026 referendum, around 70% of voters approved the charter, which proposed term limits for prime ministers, the creation of an upper house of parliament, stronger presidential powers and greater judicial independence.

The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a decisive majority in a general election that took place alongside the referendum.

Critics say the BNP has since failed to implement several pre-election reform commitments.

Ali Riaz, who led the interim government's Constitution Reform Commission, said there had been "time-bound commitments," including the creation of a constitutional reform council and steps to implement reforms within 180 working days.

"That was not done," he said, adding that it was "deeply regrettable."

Is Bangladesh moving in the wrong direction?

The interim government introduced 133 ordinances as part of its reform agenda, but after the BNP came to power, it refused to adopt 20 of them — including measures concerning the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the Anti-Corruption Commission, enforced disappearances and referendums.

The BNP argues that constitutional and institutional changes should be enacted through proper legislative procedures in Parliament.

The BNP and the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami-led alliance have clashed over the July Charter, including proposals for a constituent assembly to oversee constitutional reforms.

Salahuddin Ahmed, who led the BNP's representatives in the National Consensus Commission, now serves as Bangladesh's Home Minister.

Speaking in Parliament in March, Ahmed described the charter's implementation order as "a document of endless deception" by the interim government.

Asif Mahmud, spokesperson for the student-led National Citizen Party (NCP), accused the BNP of "betraying the public" on its reform promises and cast doubt on "whether voters would trust the party again if a similar political moment were to arise."

Mahmud, a leading figure in the uprising who later served as an adviser in the interim government before resigning ahead of the national election, told DW: "The BNP is taking the country backward by revoking the very ordinances and reforms that the interim government had implemented."

However, Khan believes the opposition party also bears responsibility for this. "It is not just the ruling party; there is no sign of the opposition breaking free from this tendency either."

While he sees some change in the way prime ministerial power is exercised, he believes "politicization has returned to major institutions, including educational ones."

Have public aspirations been realized?

Mahmud said "political parties were eager to secure power" through early elections, forcing student leaders of the uprising to "make compromises on key reform demands."

Alleged enforced disappearances were among the most serious accusations against Hasina's government. A commission set up by the interim administration reported that, of 1,913 complaints received, 1,569 were verified and classified as cases of enforced disappearance.

Among those who later returned alive, about 75% were linked to the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami and 22% to the BNP, the main political rivals of Hasina's Awami League party.

In an effort to prevent future abuses, Bangladesh signed the UN Convention against Enforced Disappearances in August 2024. The interim government later introduced an ordinance to criminalize the practice.

"We wanted to ensure permanence by incorporating this into the constitution and making the necessary legal changes," Asif Mahmud said.

However, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for the ordinance, the BNP-led government published a new draft bill in July 2026.

Critics say the proposal weakened safeguards by assigning investigations into alleged enforced disappearances from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) to the police.

Human Rights Watch (HRW)  warned that "allowing the police to investigate enforced disappearances will not ensure accountability and will not create the deterrence necessary to bring this practice to an end."

HRW also cited the April 21 alleged abduction of Miraj Sheikh by men allegedly posing as Coast Guard personnel as the first reported enforced disappearance since the 2024 uprising. More than three months later, his whereabouts remain unknown.

"We see signs of a return to those old times," Khan said. "Naturally, this is alarming."

The 'Hasina Factor' persists in Bangladesh politics

The Awami League and its affiliated organizations remain banned under an executive order and were excluded from February's elections.

Hasina, meanwhile, has been sentenced to death by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal over crimes against humanity committed during the 2024 uprising and remains self-exiled in India.

Yet despite her fall from power, Hasina and her Awami League continue to loom large over Bangladesh's political landscape.

In a Reuters interview last month, Hasina said she plans to return to Bangladesh in December and surrender to the authorities.

The authorities in Dhaka "want to take me back, they are repeatedly sending letters to India seeking to have me sent back," she said. "I will go myself."

"I believe in justice and I feel that once proceedings start, it will be ​clear to the people how farcical the court is," Hasina added, "and that I want to prove it."

The announcement of her planned return has fueled fresh debate.

NCP spokesperson Asif Mahmud argued that "even India no longer wishes to host Hasina" and suggested her remarks reflect growing uncertainty about her future there.

Mahmud added that sheltering Hasina now provides India with little political benefit and complicates relations with Bangladesh's current government.

Bangladesh's attorney general has declared that Hasina would be arrested immediately upon her return and stand trial.

Ali Riaz, however, warned that Hasina's return could create new challenges. "During the trial proceedings, she and her followers might attempt to destabilize the law-and-order situation in Bangladesh for political gain," he said, calling on the government to guard against any resulting instability.

Others, however, see a different possibility. Khan said the tensions surrounding Hasina's return could instead help "forge broader political unity in a deeply divided country."

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Guatemala: Towns evacuated as Fuego volcano erupts
entries.summary: The country's disaster agency issued its second-highest warning level and urged residents to seek shelter. Onlookers have also been warned to stop climbing a nearby volcano to take videos of the eruption.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

The country's disaster agency issued its second-highest warning level and urged residents to seek shelter. Onlookers have also been warned to stop climbing a nearby volcano to take videos of the eruption.

Guatemala's disaster management agency CONRED issued evacuation notices for several towns near the highly active Volcan de Fuego on Tuesday, as it spewed columns of lava, gas, and ash some four kilometers (2.5 miles) into the sky.

The volcano is located some 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Guatemala City.

CONRED issued an orange warning, its second-highest level, and urged residents to move to emergency shelters outside of the volcano's path. Schools have been closed in the area and some businesses have temporarily shuttered.

According to the agency, ash clouds have traveled as far as 60 kilometers (37 miles) to the west of the volcano, and could significantly disrupt air traffic in the area.

Guatemala's Institute of Seismology and Volcanology stressed that the volcano is experiencing its "most intense phase" and that people should be extremely careful with a 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) radius of it.

Hikers warned to leave area

Local media reported that onlookers continued to climb the nearby Acatenango volcano, despite a safety ban, in order to take videos of the eruption to post on social media.

Volcan de Fuego is nearly 3,800 meters (12,500 feet) tall and sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire. It is one of the most active volcanoes in Central America, and in 2018 a violent eruption claimed the lives of some 200 people.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy
entries.summary: The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy

August 4, 2026

The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.

"I think it's really important to keep the fairness in our tour," said Sabalenka on Monday. "Obviously, biologically, men are way stronger than women, so I feel like it would not be really fair for a woman to compete against a biological man.

"I believe it took them a little while to make this decision and I support it," the Belarussian continued. "If they want to test us all, I'm happy to do that; it's pretty fair, and let's keep it that way."

WTA introduces genetic testing

In July 2026, the WTA (Women's Tennis Association) introduced a one-time, mandatory genetic test for all players. As part of the protocol, players will be tested for the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome. The test can be conducted by a cheek swab or a blood test.

The new policy also includes a document players must sign highlighting disciplinary action is possible if testing is refused.

The previous WTA policy allowed transgender women to compete if their testosterone levels had been lowered to below 2.5 nmol/L continuously for the previous two years. There are no known transgender women currently playing on the WTA Tour.

Sabalenka is currently the best female tennis player in the world, and has been ranked number 1 for 92 consecutive weeks, so her endorsement carries a lot of weight.

On top of that, she competed in the modern edition of Battle of the Sexes in Dubai in 2025 — a match she lost to Nick Kyrgios, a male Australian player. While billed as a way to generate interest in tennis, some were critical of the match-up.

World Boxing introduced it in May 2025 after a lengthy and controversial debate around gold medal winner Imane Khelif at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

World Athletics did similarly in September 2025. Then, in the decision likely to have the most far-reaching impacts, the International Olympic Committee updated their guidelines in early 2026.

How has this new policy been received?

Trans athletes have long been politicized.

Riley Gaines, a former swimmer at the US collegiate level, has become a conservative political activist who is known for campaigning against the participation of trans women in women's sports. Recently, Gaines was seen supporting WNBA star Sophie Cunningham, who had said in an ESPN feature that "biological men" should not compete in female sports in order to protect young girls.

Maria Jose Martinez-Patino, whose personal experience with gender verification dramatically impacted sporting policy on the matter in the 1980s, believes new genetic testing for women at elite level is "a setback of several decades."

"It takes me back to the 1950s and 1960s, when women practically had to go through a series of controls, had to undress in front of a panel of doctors," Martinez-Patino told DW in an interview in 2025. "I get the impression that we haven't advanced from a scientific point of view. We've made practically no progress if it's now categorically said that women with X and Y chromosomes are not women."

World Athletics argues that the SRY gene — present in people with a Y chromosome, usually men — "is a reliable indicator for determining biological sex." Martinez-Patino believes, though, that determining someone's sex is not as simple as that.

"It's not black or white. There are more than 60 genetic mutations which I think are not all that complicated to study. Something that I've always said is that it should be done case by case," the Spanish former hurdler said.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: Iran: Is Reza Pahlavi's political star fading?
entries.summary: Once seen as a leading opposition figure, Pahlavi now faces questions about his political relevance in Western capitals and inside Iran.
entries.content:
Asia

Iran: Is Reza Pahlavi's political star fading?

August 4, 2026

Once seen as a leading opposition figure, Pahlavi now faces questions about his political relevance in Western capitals and inside Iran.

An investigation by Reuters news agency into Reza Pahlavi, the son of the last shah of Iran, has raised a question: has Iran's most prominent opposition figure abroad lost credibility and influence among Western policymakers and Iranians?

Reuters reported in July that Pahlavi's candidacy had "sputtered" after appearing to reach its high point earlier this year.

Although he has repeatedly declared his readiness to lead Iran through a transitional period, senior US officials have publicly distanced themselves from the prospect of a US-backed effort to bring Pahlavi to power.

The Reuters report notes that critics accuse Pahlavi of relying too heavily on foreign military intervention and failing to build a lasting political coalition.

A shift in Pahlavi's rhetoric

During periods of heightened tensions, Pahlavi welcomed international pressure on the Islamic Republic.

In January 2026, he told Iranians that the international community had entered the stage of action and echoed US President Donald Trump's message that help was "on its way."

"Great nation of Iran, the eyes of the world are upon you. Take to the streets, and as a united front, shout your demands," Pahlavi wrote on X.

After the military conflict failed to bring about the collapse of the Iranian government and criticism intensified over the consequences of war, Pahlavi said that "the final victory will still be forged by our hands" and that it was the Iranian people who would "finish the job."

The main responsibility, he said, remained with the Iranian people themselves. Some critics argued that this emphasis on the role of the Iranian people marked a retreat from his earlier messaging about international help.

How the West views Pahlavi

Mojtaba Najafi, a researcher focusing on political and social movements in Iran, argues that Western governments have never regarded Pahlavi as a truly viable option.

"A serious alternative would need the capacity to gain and manage power, influence existing power structures and offer a realistic prospect of structural political change," Najafi said. "Western governments have never considered Pahlavi to have met these criteria."

Najafi distinguishes between Europe and the United States. "European governments primarily approach Iran from the perspective of stability," he said, pointing to migration, geopolitical and security concerns, and the containment of radicalism and terrorism.

The researcher argues that, in the United States, pragmatic forces favor an accommodation with elements of the Islamic Republic.

"Their main concern is ending the regime's anti-American orientation and protecting US interests," Najafi said. "From this perspective, Washington is not necessarily seeking a transition led by a figure such as Pahlavi."

Israel's position is different

Israel's approach differs from that of the United States and Europe because Israel and the Islamic Republic have been enemies for the past few decades.

Najafi argues that some Israeli officials may view an opposition movement such as Pahlavi's as a useful source of pressure on the Islamic Republic.

Arash Azizi, a researcher at Boston University, is more critical. He argues that Pahlavi has failed to demonstrate the political skills necessary for his ambitions.

"Pahlavi has failed to demonstrate the political skills necessary for the ambitions he has set for himself," Azizi said. "His strategy has relied heavily on foreign powers that have shown little willingness to support him decisively."

"Pahlavi has cultivated ties with Western and, more recently, Israeli figures, but these efforts have not translated into decisive political backing," Azizi added.

Washington remains divided

Amir Taheri, a Paris-based political activist and supporter of constitutional monarchy, offers a more favorable assessment. He argues that Pahlavi leads a movement that has managed to connect different groups within the opposition and has been the most visible Iranian opposition figure abroad over the past year.

At the same time, Taheri acknowledges that Washington's position is divided. While parts of the Republican Party support Pahlavi, another faction favors accepting the existing political reality in Iran and seeking a new order from within the current system.

Taheri also considers Pahlavi's meetings with right-wing politicians in Europe a strategic mistake. Such contacts, he says, have not been well received by governments and traditional political forces.

His popularity in Iran remains uncertain

Pahlavi's popularity inside Iran is difficult to measure reliably. Iranian society remains highly volatile, with many people facing repression, economic hardship and inflation.

The consequences of war, Najafi argues, have shown that simplistic assumptions about political change through foreign intervention can bring suffering to the Iranian population. If the conflict does not result in political change, it could seriously damage Pahlavi's popularity.

Taheri also sees a decline in Pahlavi's political trajectory. His association with conservative and right-wing parties in the United States and Europe, as well as his support for a war that many Iranians regard as unjust, have damaged his position, he argues.

From a personal to a systemic alternative

The experts offer no unified answer to who could replace Pahlavi if his political standing continues to weaken.

Azizi and Najafi emphasize the limitations of his movement and the cautious attitude of Western governments. Neither identifies a specific alternative, instead stressing the importance of civil society and domestic forces within Iran.

Mehrdad Bozorg, a Germany-based political analyst and supporter of Reza Pahlavi, argues that Pahlavi's credibility among Iranians has actually increased, particularly following a brutal clampdown on anti-government protesters.



"After this crackdown, Iranians understood more clearly than ever that the Islamic Republic must go," Bozorg said. "At the same time, Reza Pahlavi has been the only opposition figure who has sincerely and consistently worked toward achieving a transition away from the Islamic Republic."

Bozorg said Pahlavi's legitimacy comes from the trust of the Iranian people rather than from other countries and argued that Western hesitation to acknowledge this hampers the Iranian people's aspirations for freedom.

"Israel, for various reasons, shares the Iranian people's view and, at least regarding the need for the Islamic Republic to leave power, is aligned with the national revolution movement," Bozorg said.

"It therefore sees the reality on the ground and understands that the Iranian people have chosen Reza Pahlavi as the leader of the transition. For this reason, it is realistic for Israel to view Reza Pahlavi as the only alternative."

Taheri argues that Iran should move beyond personality-driven politics and toward a "systemic alternative." In his view, the 1979 revolution's transfer of power to a single figure, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, should not be repeated.

Reza Pahlavi remains the most widely recognized Iranian opposition figure, according to many analysts. Yet there is no consensus over his political influence or his ability to unite opponents of the Islamic Republic.

While Arash Azizi and Mojtaba Najafi believe his position has weakened, Amir Taheri still considers him a major opposition actor.

Whether Pahlavi regains or further loses political weight will depend largely on Iran's evolving political landscape and the position of international powers.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Ukraine drone strikes kill five near Moscow, Russia says
entries.summary: Russian officials say Ukrainian drones have killed five people, hitting industrial and warehouse sites near Moscow and St Petersburg. Meanwhile, a soldier has killed four people in Russian-controlled Crimea. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine drone strikes kill five near Moscow, Russia says

Published August 4, 2026last updated August 4, 2026

Russian officials say Ukrainian drones have killed five people, hitting industrial and warehouse sites near Moscow and St Petersburg. Meanwhile, a soldier has killed four people in Russian-controlled Crimea. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Moscow's regional governor says five people were killed in an industrial zone
  • A warehouse facility near St Petersburg and a hub belonging to online retailer Wildberries were also said to have been hit
  • A serviceman opened fire on fellow soldiers and civilians in Crimea’s Sevastopol, killing four, with motives unclear
  • Russia says it hit targets in the Odesa region, while a drone hit a Russian cargo ship

Here is a roundup of the key developments in Russia's war in Ukraine on Tuesday, August 4, 2026:



Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Poland intercepts Russian spy plane

Poland intercepts Russian spy plane

The Polish Air Force said it had intercepted a Russian reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea.

It was the third time within a few days that such a plane had been intercepted, the government said on Tuesday.

The Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft was 56 km (34 miles) northeast of the Polish city of Koszalin, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in an online post.

Two Polish fighter jets intercepted the aircraft. An air intercept involves pilots making visual contact with the opposing crew and signal that their aircraft should move away.

The defense ministry said Polish airspace had not been violated.

"Russia is once again carrying out provocative actions near the borders of NATO member states, thereby testing the vigilance and operational readiness of the alliance's defense systems," Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote.

Skip next section Four killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine — regional authorities

Four killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine — regional authorities

At least four civilians have been killed in a fresh wave of Russian attacks on cities in northern and southern Ukraine, including two girls aged 5 and 10.

The children and a woman died in Sumy after Russian forces dropped eight guided bombs on the northeastern city, regional military chief Oleh Hryhorov said.

He said six of the bombs hit civilian sites, while Ukrainian forces intercepted two.

Further south, an 89-year-old woman was killed in Mykolaiv and seven other people were wounded, according to regional military governor Heorhii Reshetylov.

The strike also damaged homes and a vehicle.

The attacks come as fighting increasingly reaches far beyond the front line. Russia continues its invasion launched in February 2022, while Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes on targets deep inside Russian territory.

Skip next section Turkey condemns attacks on civilian shipping in Black Sea

Turkey condemns attacks on civilian shipping in Black Sea

Turkey has strongly condemned the growing threat to civilian shipping in the Black Sea after drone attacks on two Turkish-owned vessels left several crew members injured.

The Foreign Ministry said the Yasar and Nadezhda were attacked after leaving the Russian port of Novorossiysk late on Monday, adding that the condition of those wounded was being "closely monitored."

"We are deeply concerned about the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea, which is affecting civilian shipping despite our numerous warnings," the ministry said.

Ankara called on both sides to "urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea," warning that continued attacks could endanger not only commercial shipping but also food supplies.

Turkey has repeatedly raised the alarm over attacks on civilian vessels as Russia and Ukraine step up strikes on shipping in the region.

A Turkish fishing vessel was attacked near Crimea in late June, killing one person and injuring four others.

At the end of May, Ankara warned of an "uncontrolled escalation" in the Black Sea after another Turkish cargo ship was struck by a drone. Ukraine's navy said at the time that a Russian drone had carried out that attack.

Skip next section Ukraine accuses Russia of hunting civilians with drones

Ukraine accuses Russia of hunting civilians with drones

Ukrainian authorities have accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after police released video appearing to show a drone chasing a man through the streets of Kherson.

The footage shows a man running around a vehicle as a first-person-view drone follows him before detonating its explosive charge.

Police said the 52-year-old suffered injuries and a concussion.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the incident a "barbaric war crime committed by Russia" and said thousands of similar cases never become public.

"This is a deliberate and systemic Russian strategy. They know exactly what they are doing," he wrote on X.

Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said the man in the video was an "unarmed market vendor."

"The world must watch without looking away," he said. "This is how Russia hunts civilians. If anyone still asks who Russia considers its target, the answer is in this footage.

"This is not war. It is deliberate terror against civilians. It is yet another Russian war crime that must receive a proper international legal assessment."

Kherson, which had around 280,000 residents before the war, was occupied by Russian forces from March to November 2022, after which it was retaken in a Ukrainian counter-offensive.

Russian troops are now positioned across the Dnipro River from the city and regularly strike it, including with drones.

Skip next section Ukraine's former army chief says NATO membership unlikely

Ukraine's former army chief says NATO membership unlikely

Ukraine's former top military commander Valery Zaluzhnyi has said the country is unlikely ever to join NATO, despite membership remaining a constitutional goal.

Zaluzhnyi, now Ukraine's ambassador to Britain, told a meeting of Ukrainian ambassadors that the country's armed forces did not meet the military standards required for membership.

"I know NATO really well. For about 12 years, I personally worked on making sure we met NATO standards, and every year I heard tales about how we would join NATO any day now," Ukrainian media outlet European Pravda quoted him as saying.

"Unfortunately, we will never actually join."

Zaluzhnyi said Ukraine's military remained too far behind in areas including missile defense and space capabilities.

Ukraine has written its ambition to join both NATO and the European Union into its constitution, although Kyiv has acknowledged that not all NATO members currently support its accession.

Zaluzhnyi was dismissed as Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024 after disagreements with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the conduct of the war with Russia. He remains one of Ukraine's most trusted public figures, with opinion polls putting him roughly level with Zelenskyy.

Skip next section Russia says it struck Ukrainian ports and cargo ships

Russia says it struck Ukrainian ports and cargo ships

Russia's Defense Ministry says its forces have carried out a series of strikes on Ukrainian ports and vessels it claimed were carrying military cargo.

The ministry said precision weapons and drones hit targets in the southwestern Odesa region, including the Chornomorsk Automotive Components Plant and a port terminal in Chornomorsk.

It claimed Ukrainian forces were using the sites to repair military vehicles and store ammunition and fuel.

Russia also said two dry-cargo ships were struck in the ports of Mykolaiv and Pivdennyi.

The ministry subsequently said two more dry-cargo vessels were hit at sea south of Odesa while transporting weapons and military equipment to Ukrainian ports.

Skip next section Three seriously injured in drone strike on cargo ship

Three seriously injured in drone strike on cargo ship

Three crew members have been seriously injured after a cargo ship was hit in a drone attack near Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, according to Turkey's maritime authority.

The roll-on/roll-off vessel Nadezhda was sailing from Novorossiysk to the northern Turkish port of Samsun when it came under attack on Monday around 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) offshore.

All 22 crew members were evacuated to Russia, including the three seriously injured sailors.

A fire was still burning in the bow of the vessel after the attack, the Turkish authority said.

Skip next section Four killed in Sevastopol shooting

Four killed in Sevastopol shooting

Four people have been killed after a serviceman opened fire in the Russian-controlled Crimean city of Sevastopol, according to the Moscow-installed governor.

Mikhail Razvozhayev said the attacker first shot at fellow servicemen, killing one and injuring another.

The gunman then turned his weapon on civilians, killing three more people, Razvozhayev wrote on the messaging platform Telegram.

The attacker was detained, he said.

The serviceman's nationality and motive were not immediately clear.

Sevastopol was illegally innexed by Russia in 2014 alongside the rest of the Crimean Peninsula

Skip next section Ukrainian drone strikes kill five near Moscow

Ukrainian drone strikes kill five near Moscow

Ukrainian drone attacks have killed five people and injured at least seven others in Russia, striking industrial and warehouse sites near Moscow and St Petersburg.

Moscow regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said several fires broke out after drones hit the Novoselki industrial zone outside the capital.

"According to preliminary information, five people were killed and a further six wounded," he said on Telegram.

A warehouse also caught fire in the attack before firefighters brought the blaze under control.

Near St Petersburg, drones damaged a warehouse facility in Krasny Bor, injuring one person, Leningrad regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said.

The Leningrad region surrounds the city of St Petersburg but does not include it.

Russian online retailer Wildberries later said its logistics center there had caught fire as a result of the strike, but reported no casualties among its staff.

Ukraine has intensified long-range drone attacks on targets inside Russia in recent weeks, including logistics sites and warehouses.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Moscow's regional governor says Ukrainian drones struck the Novoselki industrial zone outside the Russian capital.

Five people are reported to have been killed, with other industrial and warehouse sites near Russia's two largest cities also hit.

Russian online retailer Wildberries says one of its facilities was among those hit and caught fire as a result.

Meanwhile, four people have been killed in a mysterious shooting in the Russian-controlled Crimean city of Sevastopol, according to a Moscow-installed official.

Stay with us for the latest on these stories and other developments in Russia's war in Ukraine.
